1: In the last week of April 1929, in the same Dutch province, two girls were born four days apart. One of them was called Wil de Groot. Her father repaired bicycles in a town about nineteen kilometres from where the other girl's family kept a house, and her mother had worked in a bakery until the week before, and nothing about the arrival was remarkable. The other girl's family had a title, a great deal of complicated property, and connections in two countries, and her birth was noted in a newspaper. Neither of them ever met the other. Neither of them, as far as anybody has been able to establish, ever knew the other existed. What makes them worth putting side by side is not the coincidence of dates, and it is certainly not the shape people expect — one life a success, the other a quiet tragedy in the background. That version is wrong. They were both very good dancers. They were both taught by women who had trained in the same tradition. Both of them spent the winter of 1944 hungry in an occupied country, roughly forty minutes apart by bicycle if there had been a bicycle to spare. And in the spring of 1948, within about five weeks of each other, both of them auditioned in London for the same kind of work. Both were turned down. The thing that separated them arrived after that, and it was not talent, and it was not character, and it took about four weeks. This is the story of two lives that ran parallel for nineteen years, came within nineteen kilometres of each other twice, and then went in directions that had almost nothing to do with either of the two girls involved.
2: Take 1935 first, when they were both six, because the difference at that age is smaller than it ever is again. Both were in school. Both were considered clever by teachers who wrote it down. Wil was the better reader by a distance and was moved up a year, which produced a certificate her mother kept until 1979. The other girl was moved between countries instead, twice, for reasons that had to do with her parents rather than with her, and the interruption cost her most of a year of schooling. If you were making a prediction in 1935 about which of these two would end up with a career, and you had only the school records in front of you, you would have picked Wil, and you would have been reasoning correctly from the available evidence. The story people like about talent is that it declares itself early and unmistakably, and in 1935 the more obviously gifted of these two was the bicycle repairer's daughter. Both started ballet in the same year, 1937, at eight. Wil's lessons were paid for by an aunt. They cost, per term, about what her father earned in nine days, and there is a note in the aunt's account book about it that survives, and the note is not sentimental. It says the amount and the word yes. Nine days of a man's wages, agreed to in one word by a relative who is otherwise absent from this entire story, is the kind of decision that turns out to have been enormous and that nobody involved could have known it. The other girl's lessons were arranged without any comparable difficulty and without anybody writing anything down, because that is what money is: it is the absence of a note in an account book.
3: Nineteen forty-four is where the two lives come closest in physical distance and stop being comparable in any other way. Both were fifteen. Both were in the occupied part of the country when the food stopped. Both ate things that are not food. Wil lost her father in February 1945, not to a firing squad but to pneumonia in a house with no fuel, which is how most of that winter's dead actually died. The other girl lost an uncle to the firing squad two years earlier and almost never spoke about it. Here is the part that resists being turned into a lesson: the winter did roughly the same physical damage to both. Both had oedema. Both had the respiratory trouble afterward. Both were left thin in a way a certain kind of person would later call elegant in one case and undernourished in the other, which tells you about that kind of person and nothing about the two girls. In April 1945 they were nineteen kilometres apart and neither of them could have walked it. There is one more thing about that winter and it cuts against the way this kind of comparison usually goes. The family with the title did not eat better. Property is not food, and in the occupied Netherlands in the winter of 1944 a great house with nothing in the cellar was in some ways worse off than a small one near a farm, because the small one had neighbours who owed nothing and helped anyway. Wil's household got potatoes twice from a farm four fields away. The other household, by every account, got nothing from anybody, because nobody in that district thought a family like that would need it and nobody wanted to be the one to ask.
4: Nineteen forty-eight, London, five weeks apart, and the beginning of the divergence that everybody assumes must have been there all along. Both auditioned for the chorus. Both were seen by people who wrote assessments down. Wil's assessment survives, in a company's papers, and it says that she was technically the stronger of the applicants seen that day, with an unusually good line, and that she was rejected. The reason is written next to it and it is four words long: too old to train. She was nineteen. In 1948, in that world, nineteen was too old to begin the years of work that turn a very good dancer into a professional one, and the assessment is not cruel, it is a straightforward statement of how the profession worked. The other girl was rejected too, by two companies, for the same reason and in almost the same words, and this is the fact that the success story leaves out. The difference between them arrived afterward and it was not talent and it was not character. One of them was in a city where a second kind of work existed, was noticed in a chorus line by somebody who was casting something else, and was asked whether she had ever considered acting. The other one went home, because she could not afford to stay in London and wait. Read those two sentences again and notice what is not in them. There is no moment of daring. Neither girl did anything decisive. One of them was standing in a particular line on a particular afternoon when a man with a different job walked past it, and the other one was on a train, and the train was not a decision either. It was a ticket that was about to expire.
5: That sentence is the hinge and deserves looking at directly. Wil went home because the money ran out. She had six weeks in London on savings and an aunt's contribution, and at the end of them she had two more auditions that had not yet happened and no way to stay for them. She wrote in a letter at the time — the only letter from that period that survives — that she thought she had another year in her if she could get back the following season, and she did not get back the following season, because her mother was alone and there was work in a canning factory. She was nineteen years old. Nobody made a decision about her; nobody even had an opinion. The other girl stayed in London because her mother was in London, in a flat, with a job, and staying cost her nothing she did not already have. That is the difference. Not courage, not hunger, not some private quality that reveals itself under pressure. An address, and a mother in the right city, and consequently four more weeks of being available in a season when somebody happened to be looking. It is worth being stubborn about this, because the alternative explanations are all more flattering and all worse. Not that one wanted it more — Wil's letter is the letter of somebody who wanted it a great deal. Not that one was tougher; they had survived the identical winter. Not even luck, in any useful sense, because luck implies a roll of something and there was no roll. There was a rent book. One girl had four weeks of somewhere to sleep that cost her nothing and the other did not, and every single thing that happened afterward to either of them proceeds from that.
6: What happened to Wil de Groot between 1949 and 1991 takes about a paragraph to summarise and that is not an insult to it. She worked in the canning factory for two years. She married a man named Joop who drove a delivery lorry, in 1952, and they had three children between 1953 and 1959. She taught ballet. That is the part that gets left out when this story is told badly, because it is assumed she must have stopped: she did not stop, she taught, in a room above a shop in her own town, two evenings a week from 1955 until 1988, which is thirty-three years, and something in the region of four hundred children passed through that room. Two of them became professionals. One of those two, a girl called Annemarie who started with her in 1966 at the age of seven, danced with a company in Germany for eleven years, and said in an interview in 1994 that she had had exactly one teacher who mattered and that the woman had never been anywhere or done anything and had been the best teacher in the country. Wil kept her father's bicycle tools. She was, by every account of her, a cheerful and rather sharp-tongued woman with no visible sense of grievance at all. Her pupils remembered two things in particular. She would not let a child work on anything showy until the plain things were correct, which made her unpopular for about a year with every one of them. And she never once, in thirty-three years, told a child they could not do it — nor, several noticed later, that they could. She told them what to do next week, and the ones who asked about their prospects got an answer about their feet.
7: The obvious question is whether she knew, and the answer is that of course she knew, in the way that everybody in Europe knew by about 1955 — from a poster, from a magazine at a hairdresser's, from her own pupils talking about a film. She was asked about it, once, in 1990, by a local paper doing a piece on her retirement, and the question was put in the tactless way local papers put things, which was whether she ever thought about how close she had come. She said that she had not come close to anything. She said the comparison was not a real one, that they had never been in competition because they had never been in the same room, and that a person who spends her life measuring it against a life she did not have is going to do a bad job of the one she has. Then she said the part that got printed and that her family were not entirely happy about, which was that she had watched two or three of the films and had thought that the woman was very good and that it was obviously the right decision by whoever made it, and that this was not modesty, it was simply her opinion as somebody who had spent thirty-three years watching people dance and move. Her eldest daughter said the family winced at the printed version because it read as humility, and humility had nothing to do with it. What her mother actually said at home, more bluntly, was that the two of them had been asked entirely different questions and that comparing the answers was a category error. She used the phrase. She had left school at fifteen, read four or five books a month for fifty years, and talked like that when she was annoyed.
8: They died two years apart. The other girl in January 1993, in Switzerland, and it was on television in every country in Europe. Wil de Groot in March 1995, in the same town she was born in, and there were about ninety people at the funeral, which for a woman of sixty-five in a town that size is a great many. Annemarie came from Germany. So did four other former pupils and the daughters of a fifth. There is no moral available here, and the reason to put the two lives side by side is not to produce one. It is that the distance between them was four weeks of rent in the spring of 1948, and that the one who did not get the four weeks spent the following four decades doing something that four hundred children and at least one professional company were the better for, and that neither of those facts diminishes the other in the slightest. If there is anything to take from putting them together, it is probably the thing Wil herself said to the local paper, which is that a life measured against a life you did not have is a life done badly. She was not saying it to be brave. She was saying it as a technical observation, in the same voice she used to tell a nine-year-old that the plain things come first, and she had thirty-three years and four hundred children behind the remark. The room above the shop is a dentist's waiting area now. There is no plaque, and if you asked in the town today most people would not know the name, and Annemarie, who is in her sixties, still uses the exercise Wil built for her in 1971 when her ankles are bad. This story is a work of fiction. Wil, Annemarie, Joop and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
